opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest with yourself about what you cannot do. If you're a small team, you're not going to win by training the biggest foundation model. That game is about compute, data, and capital, and the large companies have all three in quantities that are hard to match. So if you try to fight them head-on on the same axis, you'll probably lose, and you'll lose expensively.

But I don't think that means small players have no chance. Actually, I think there are a few places where being small is an advantage.

One is focus. A big company has to serve everyone, so their models and products are general by design. A small team can pick one problem and go extremely deep: a specific domain, a specific kind of agent, a specific workflow, and do it much better than a general system would. In my own work on reinforcement learning and agents, I've seen that the last mile often matters most. The base model gives you capability, but turning that into something that reliably solves a real task needs a lot of careful engineering, good environment design, and good reward design. That work doesn't scale automatically with compute, and big companies often don't prioritize it.

The second is speed and taste. In a fast-moving field, the ability to make a bet quickly and change direction quickly is very valuable. A small team can try an unconventional idea without going through layers of approval. Many important ideas in AI looked a bit strange at first. If you have good research taste and you move fast, you can find those things before they become consensus.

The third is to build on top of the big players rather than against them. Open-source models are now strong enough that you can stand on their shoulders. Let the large companies spend billions pushing the frontier of pretraining, then you focus on post-training, RL, agent systems, infrastructure, or applications where you create unique value. In some sense their progress becomes your tailwind.

I'd add one more thing: talent density matters more than headcount. A small group of people who really understand the full stack, from algorithms to systems, can do surprising things. In my experience, a few strong people with a clear goal can often outperform a much larger team that's spread thin.

So my short answer: don't compete on scale. Compete on focus, speed, depth, and taste, and pick a battlefield where those things are decisive.

r001.rationale: The response recommends that small teams focus deeply on a specific domain, problem, or workflow where they can outperform general systems, and notes that large companies often do not prioritize this last-mile work.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest about what you can't do. A small team can't win on compute, can't win on data scale, can't win on the number of GPUs you can line up. If you try to compete on the same axis as the big labs, you've basically already lost, because they have ten or a hundred times your resources and they're not going to stop spending.

So the question becomes: where does scale not matter, or even become a disadvantage? And I think there are a few places.

One is speed and focus. A large company has many teams, many priorities, and a lot of internal coordination cost. A small team can pick one narrow problem and go all the way to the end on it. When I was working on reinforcement learning, a lot of the interesting results didn't come from the biggest model, they came from somebody who had a very specific insight about the training signal or the environment and just iterated faster than anyone else. Big companies are often slow to go deep on something that isn't obviously on the main roadmap.

Second is the application layer and the real world. The foundation models are becoming more and more similar. The differentiation increasingly comes from understanding a specific domain, a specific user, a specific workflow, and from the data you collect by actually deploying. That kind of data is not something you can buy with more GPUs. It comes from being close to users and being willing to do things that don't look glamorous.

Third, I think small players should take research risk that big companies won't. Large labs are, to some degree, in an arms race on known recipes, scaling what already works. There's less appetite for things that might take two years and might fail. If you're small, you have nothing to protect, so you can place bets on different architectures, different training paradigms, agents, embodied systems, whatever. Most of those bets will fail, but the ones that don't are how you become relevant.

And finally, I'd say don't underestimate talent density. A team of ten people who truly understand the problem can still outperform a team of a hundred who are just executing. The big labs know this too, which is why they pay so much. But a lot of very good people prefer a small environment where they can own something, and that's a real recruiting advantage if you build the right culture.

So, in short: don't fight them where they're strong. Pick a narrow problem, move fast, get close to real users, and be willing to take the research risks that the large companies are structurally unable to take.

r001.rationale: The response recommends that small teams focus on narrow problems and areas where large companies are slow or structurally less able to compete effectively.

astra-6.text:
I think smaller players have to be very clear about where their advantage comes from. If you try to do exactly what a large company does, but with less compute, less data, and fewer people, that’s a very difficult competition.

But AI is a very broad field. A small team can focus on a specific problem, understand the users deeply, and iterate much faster. The goal is to find something where insight and execution matter more than scale. You might serve a particular industry or solve a workflow that a large company doesn’t prioritize.

You also have to think about what happens when the underlying models improve. If a better model makes your product unnecessary, that’s a fragile position. Ideally, better models make your product more useful, because your value comes from understanding the problem and making the technology work in practice.

So I would focus less on competing with large companies in general, and more on finding a problem that a small team can solve exceptionally well.

r001.rationale: The response recommends focusing on specific problems or workflows that large companies do not prioritize, where a small team’s user insight and faster iteration can provide an advantage.

sol-6.1.text:
I think smaller AI players need to be very clear about where their advantage comes from. If you compete directly with a large company on the same product, and success mainly depends on compute and capital, that’s a difficult position.

But a small team can focus on a specific problem, get close to users, and iterate quickly. You might understand a particular workflow much better than a large company does. Then the question becomes: can you solve that problem substantially better, even using models that everyone has access to?

You also need to think about what happens when the underlying models improve. Does that make your product more useful, or does it eliminate the reason your product exists? I would look for opportunities where better models strengthen the value you provide. Start with a narrow problem, demonstrate real value, and expand from there.

r001.rationale: The response recommends focusing on a specific problem or workflow where a small team can understand users better and solve the problem substantially better than a large company.
